item.title: Scientists Can Now Spot Hidden Sunspots on the Solar Far Side
item.description: Unlike the Moon, the Sun is constantly rotating from our perspective - but we still only see half of it at any given time. Since it takes 27 days to complete a full rotation, that leaves plenty of time for changes to happen to the side we can’t see that could directly impact Earth’s own space weather a few weeks later. item.title: Tiny ‘solar flares’ recreated in the lab may explain corona mystery
item.description: An experiment has produced nanoflares similar to those seen on the sun, and shown that they can help explain why the outer layers of the solar atmosphere are so hot

item.title: Parker Solar Probe Spots Twisted Magnetic Braids Growing in the Solar Wind
item.description: The magnetic environment around the Sun is a jumbled mess of chaotic fields and streams of charged particles. item.title: How flare ribbons reveal hidden solar explosions on the sun
item.description: Many topics in astronomy and astrophysics are esoteric. There's not much of a relationship between something like the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way and the life of a regular person going about their business. But the sun is different. Its presence in our lives is inescapable. Its behavior, especially its flaring, has an impact.

item.title: Laser-blasted plasma shows how instabilities could heat the sun's corona
item.description: From its visible surface, the sun radiates heat at a relatively cool temperature of 5,800 Kelvin. Yet within the thin outer layer of the sun's atmosphere known as the corona, electrons can reach temperatures of millions of degrees, for reasons astronomers have yet to fully explain.

item.title: The Largest Canyon in the Solar System is Still Tectonically Active
item.description: Scientists at Imperial College London and Columbia University have found that the largest canyon system in the solar system is still active and shaping Mars today, billions of years after it first formed.

item.title: Solar Orbiter tracks origin of mysterious magnetic switchbacks
item.description: The European Space Agency-led Solar Orbiter spacecraft has flown through an S-shaped kink known as a ‘switchback’ in the solar wind’s magnetic field. By fingerprinting the elusive particles within the switchback, Solar Orbiter has traced its origin back to the Sun’s surface and revealed more about solar magnetism – the unruly instigator of dangerous solar storms.

item.title: Total solar eclipse 2026 (Official ESA broadcast)
item.description: Video: 01:10:42 We broadcast live from the Observatorio Astrofísico de Javalambre in Spain as a total solar eclipse crossed Europe on 12 August 2026. The path of totality swept across Greenland, Iceland, Spain and a small area of northeastern Portugal, while much of Europe experienced a partial eclipse.
